analysis:
The PR only touches console-ui, a changelog and tests. It has no provider, WebSocket, attestation, key, or cache changes, so T-041/TB-007 are unaffected.

Behavior change in DeviceLinkForm.tsx: the form now takes a `purpose` prop ('provider' default, or 'desktop_account') and sends it in the POST /api/device/approve body, replacing the old `{user_code}`-only body. The UI copy adapts to the purpose. For desktop it says 'read-only, 30-day access'.

The client checks `data.purpose === 'desktop_account'` after a successful approval and shows an error otherwise. This is UX only. Authorization is enforced server-side, which per the changelog rejects a purpose/code mismatch.

The proxy test in account-proxy-contracts.test.ts confirms the Next route forwards the raw body and the bearer header unchanged. The purpose therefore reaches the coordinator unmodified.

Things the next pass should examine:
(1) The `purpose` value comes from the URL query string, via useSearchParams in link/page.tsx. That file is NOT in the supplied units, so how it parses and whitelists the value before passing it to DeviceLinkForm is unverified. An attacker-supplied link can pick the consent text. Phishing of device codes is a pre-existing class. The server-side purpose-mismatch check is the real guard.
(2) The '30-day, read-only' consent text is hardcoded in the client and could drift from the coordinator's actual grant (platform-owned, out of scope here).
(3) If an old coordinator ignores `purpose`, approval may already have happened when the client shows its error. This is low severity and not a regression of an in-scope threat.

I found no concrete security regression in the supplied diff.
